Day 1 opens with visualisation at 11:15. Work through this page first and that
will not be the first `ggplot()` call you have ever written. You will be
recognising a plot you have already drawn, rather than meeting one cold.

Every ggplot2 plot is built from three parts, and you have to name all three:

1. the **data**: which table,
2. the **aesthetics**: which column goes on which part of the picture,
3. the **geom**: what shape to draw.

Miss one and you get a blank panel rather than an error, which is confusing the
first time. So we will add them one at a time and watch the picture appear. For
the full explanation of any of this, see [the R primer](r-primer.qmd).

## 1. Data: which table

`ggplot()` on its own gives you a grey rectangle. That is not a failure. It is
R saying *I have your data and no instructions about what to do with it*.

```{webr}
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(students)
```

That is the same 240-student cohort, read with the same `read_csv()` line, from
the same `data/meded_students.csv` path you will type on Day 1.

## 2. Aesthetics: which column goes where

`aes()` maps a **column** onto a **feature of the picture**: the x axis, the y
axis, the colour, the fill. Map `attendance_pct` to x and an axis appears,
correctly scaled to the range of the data:

```{webr}
ggplot(students, aes(x = attendance_pct))
```

Still no bars, because we have not yet said what to draw. But look at the axis:
ggplot2 has already read the column, found it runs from about 57 to 100, and
chosen the breaks for you.

## 3. Geom: what shape to draw

`geom_histogram()` cuts a numeric column into bins and draws a bar per bin. It
is the standard first look at any single number.

```{webr}
ggplot(students, aes(x = attendance_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```

Attendance clusters around 80%, with a tail of students below 65%, the ones a
course convenor would want to know about. One line of code and you have seen
something you could not see in the spreadsheet.

::: {.callout-important title="`+`, not `|>`: the one exception you will meet"}
Everywhere else in the workshop you join steps with the native pipe `|>`. In
ggplot2 you join **layers** with `+`.

This is history, not logic: ggplot2 was written in 2007, years before R had a
pipe, and it already had its own way of stacking one layer onto another. It was
never changed, because millions of lines of published code use `+`.

The rule that keeps you out of trouble:

- `|>` moves a table from one **verb** to the next: `filter()`, `mutate()`,
  `summarise()`.
- `+` adds a **layer or setting** to a plot you have already started with
  `ggplot()`.

You can use both in the same expression, and often will: pipe the data into
`ggplot()`, then add layers with `+`.

```r
students |>
  filter(batch == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = attendance_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)
```

Getting these the wrong way round produces one of two errors. `ggplot(...) |>
geom_histogram()` complains about a missing argument; `students + ggplot(...)`
says *non-numeric argument to binary operator*. Everybody does it once. Now you
know what the message means.
:::

## Bin width changes what you see

`binwidth` is not a detail. It decides how much of the shape of the data
survives. Change the `2` below to `5`, then to `10`, and rerun each time:

```{webr}
ggplot(students, aes(x = attendance_pct)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2)
```

At 2 the histogram is spiky and you can see individual clumps of students; at 10
it is smooth and you may have flattened away something real. There is no correct
answer, which is exactly why you should look at more than one before you decide
what the data says.

## Comparing two groups

The workshop cohort has two teaching arms, so the obvious question is whether
they differ. A boxplot puts one box per group side by side: the thick line is
the median, the box holds the middle half of the students, and the dots beyond
the whiskers are outliers.

`fill = teaching_arm` maps the group onto the colour of the boxes;
`scale_fill_manual()` then says which colour each group gets. These are the
conclave's own two colours.

```{webr}
ggplot(students, aes(x = teaching_arm, y = burnout_score, fill = teaching_arm)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Flipped classroom"   = "#0f5257",
                               "Traditional lecture" = "#b8860b")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Burnout score", fill = NULL)
```

Two boxes, and they sit at almost the same height: median burnout is 49.7 in
the flipped arm against 49.1 in the traditional one. That is a real and useful
finding: *no visible difference* is a result, and seeing it in ten seconds is
better than testing for it in ten minutes.

`x = NULL` inside `labs()` removes an axis title that would only repeat the
group names underneath it. `fill = NULL` removes the legend title for the same
reason. Deleting labels that say nothing is most of what makes a figure look
professional.

::: {.callout-warning title="The warning under that plot is not an error"}
ggplot2 printed something like *Removed 7 rows containing non-finite outside the
scale range*. Seven students in this cohort have no `burnout_score`: the value
is `NA`, R's marker for missing, and you cannot draw a box around a value that
does not exist, so ggplot2 dropped them and told you so.

A **warning** means *I did it, here is something you should know*. An **error**
means *I could not do it, there is no result*. Beginners often stop at the first
warning; read it instead, and check the number it gives you is the number of
missing values you expected.
:::

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_hist
#|   - ex_scatter
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

students <- read_csv("data/meded_students.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: a histogram that explains itself"}
**Time:** 10 minutes

Draw a histogram of `pretest`, the score every student sat before the course
began. Then give it a title and readable axis labels with `labs()`, so that
somebody who has never seen the dataset can understand the figure on its own.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_hist
ggplot(students, aes(x = ______)) +
  ______(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(______)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_hist
#| solution: true
ggplot(students, aes(x = pretest)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  labs(
    title = "Pre-test scores across the 2022–2024 cohort",
    x = "Pre-test score (%)",
    y = "Number of students"
  )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_hist
#| check: true
# aes() is equally valid on the plot or on the layer, so look in both places.
mapped_x <- function(p) {
  from_plot <- if (!is.null(p$mapping$x)) rlang::as_label(p$mapping$x) else NULL
  from_layers <- unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) {
    if (!is.null(l$mapping$x)) rlang::as_label(l$mapping$x) else NULL
  }))
  c(from_plot, from_layers)
}
if (!inherits(.result, "ggplot")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That did not produce a plot. If there is a red error above, read that first: a geom you were not asked for, such as geom_point(), needs a y as well as an x. Otherwise, start with ggplot(students, aes(x = pretest)).")
} else if (!("pretest" %in% mapped_x(.result))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Map pretest to x inside aes().")
} else if (!any(vapply(.result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomBar"), logical(1)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Add geom_histogram() to draw the bars.")
} else if (is.null(.result$labels$title)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Nearly. Add labs(title = ...) so the plot explains itself.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct, and it has a title, which most published figures do not.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_hist"}
Three blanks, three parts. The column name goes inside `aes(x = )` with no
quotation marks. The geom is `geom_histogram`. `labs()` takes named arguments
separated by commas (`title = "..."`, `x = "..."`, `y = "..."`) and the label
text *is* quoted, because it is ordinary English rather than a column name.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: a scatter plot in three mappings"}
**Time:** 10 minutes

Do students who study more gain more? Put `study_hours` on the x axis and
`gain` on the y axis, colour the points by `rural_background`, and draw them
with `geom_point()`.

This one maps three columns at once, which is the moment `aes()` starts to earn
its keep. Expect a warning about eleven removed rows: `gain` is missing for the
eleven students who never sat the post-test.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_scatter
ggplot(students, aes(x = ______, y = ______, colour = ______)) +
  ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_scatter
#| solution: true
ggplot(students, aes(x = study_hours, y = gain, colour = rural_background)) +
  geom_point()
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_scatter
#| check: true
# aes() is equally valid on the plot or on the layer, so look in both places.
mapped <- function(p, aesthetic) {
  from_plot <- if (!is.null(p$mapping[[aesthetic]])) rlang::as_label(p$mapping[[aesthetic]]) else NULL
  from_layers <- unlist(lapply(p$layers, function(l) {
    if (!is.null(l$mapping[[aesthetic]])) rlang::as_label(l$mapping[[aesthetic]]) else NULL
  }))
  c(from_plot, from_layers)
}
if (!inherits(.result, "ggplot")) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That did not produce a plot. If there is a red error above, read that first. Otherwise, start with ggplot(students, aes(...)) and add a geom with +.")
} else if (!("study_hours" %in% mapped(.result, "x"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Map study_hours to x inside aes().")
} else if (!("gain" %in% mapped(.result, "y"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Map gain to y inside aes(), next to the x mapping and separated by a comma.")
} else if (!("rural_background" %in% mapped(.result, "colour"))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Map rural_background to colour inside aes(). For points it is colour, not fill: fill colours an area, colour draws a line or a dot.")
} else if (!any(vapply(.result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint"), logical(1)))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The mappings are right, but nothing is being drawn yet. Add + geom_point().")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct, and read what it shows: a shapeless cloud. More study hours did not mean more gain in this cohort, and the rural and urban points are mixed right through each other. A scatter plot that shows no relationship has still told you something.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_scatter"}
All three mappings go inside the one `aes()`, separated by commas. The last
blank is a whole layer, so it needs its brackets: `geom_point()`.

If you type `color` rather than `colour`, ggplot2 accepts it and quietly
converts it to `colour`, and both spellings work everywhere in the package.
:::
:::
